headings.title: Introduction to Biochemical Assessment in Nutrition
headings.content: Biochemical assessment involves measuring nutrients or their metabolites in body fluids, primarily blood and urine. While dietary histories and physical exams tell us what a patient eats and how they look, laboratory tests provide objective, measurable data. This branch of nutritional assessment uncovers early subclinical deficiencies long before physical signs like hair loss or skin changes appear. Nurses play a vital role in preparing patients, ensuring proper sample collection, and recognizing when metabolic derangements require dietary intervention.

headings.title: Assessment of Protein-Energy Malnutrition
headings.content:
Proteins are fundamental markers for evaluating visceral protein status, though their levels fluctuate based on factors beyond pure nutrition. 

- **Albumin**: The most abundant circulating protein. It has a long half-life of roughly 20 days, making it poor for detecting acute or sudden nutritional changes, but useful for monitoring chronic protein-energy depletion.
- **Prealbumin (Transthyretin)**: Features a much shorter half-life of about 2 days. Because of this rapid turnover, it responds quickly to changes in protein intake, serving as a sensitive short-term indicator of nutritional repletion.
- **Transferrin**: An iron-transport protein with a half-life of 8 to 10 days. Its levels drop during protein depletion, though iron deficiency itself can falsely elevate transferrin synthesis.

headings.title: Hematological Tests for Anemia and Nutritional Status
headings.content: Blood tests reveal vital clues about oxygen-carrying capacity and specific nutrient shortages. Hemoglobin and hematocrit provide broad screens for anemia, while red blood cell indices help pinpoint the root cause. Mean Corpuscular Volume measures the average size of red blood cells. A low MCV points toward microcytic anemia, typically caused by iron deficiency. A high MCV indicates macrocytic anemia, commonly linked to vitamin B12 or folate deficiencies. Ferritin serves as the primary storage protein for iron, representing the most sensitive test for iron deficiency anemia.

headings.title: Evaluation of Micronutrient Status
headings.content: Vitamins and minerals regulate countless metabolic reactions. Assessing them directly involves measuring serum levels, urinary excretion, or functional assays. Fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K accumulate in tissues, and serum tests can catch toxicities as well as deficiencies. Water-soluble vitamins like Vitamin C and the B-complex group wash out of the body more readily, requiring frequent intake. Minerals such as potassium, sodium, calcium, and magnesium are tightly regulated by homeostatic mechanisms, meaning serum levels can appear normal even when total body stores are depleted.

headings.title: Inflammatory Markers and Their Impact on Nutritional Biomarkers
headings.content: Inflammation drastically alters the liver's production of plasma proteins. During acute or chronic stress, the body releases cytokines that increase positive acute-phase reactants like C-reactive protein while suppressing negative acute-phase reactants like albumin, prealbumin, and transferrin. When a patient has high CRP, low albumin does not automatically mean they are malnourished; it often reflects an active inflammatory response. Nurses must check inflammatory markers alongside nutritional lab values to avoid misdiagnosing simple inflammation as protein malnutrition.

headings.title: Limitations and Confounding Factors in Biochemical Testing
headings.content: Interpreting nutritional labs requires careful clinical judgment because many non-nutritional factors skew the data. Hydration status is a major confounder: severe dehydration concentrates blood, artificially raising lab values, while fluid overload dilutes them, making modest deficiencies look catastrophic. Renal and hepatic diseases impair the metabolism and excretion of nutrients and carrier proteins. Medications, recent surgeries, and physical trauma also alter biochemical profiles. Therefore, lab values must always be interpreted alongside the patient's full clinical picture.
